Here’s an example `pytest`-style test module that covers

• A variety of known-good (“happy path”) emails  
• Clearly invalid emails  
• Some weird edge-cases that the regex as written actually accepts  
• Non-string inputs that should all raise a `TypeError`

Save this as `test_email_validator.py` (assuming your function lives in `email_validator.py` next to it).

```python
import pytest
from email_validator import is_valid_email


# ------------------
# HAPPY PATHS
# ------------------
@pytest.mark.parametrize("email", [
    # very standard
    "user@example.com",
    "USER@EXAMPLE.COM",
    "user.name+tag+sorting@example.com",
    "user_name-123@example-domain.co.uk",
    # minimal local / domain / tld
    "u@e.co",
    # two-letter and multi-letter TLDs
    "alice@wonder.land",
    "bob@razor.sh",
    "charlie@longtld.company",
])
def test_valid_emails(email):
    assert is_valid_email(email)


# ------------------
# CLEARLY INVALID ADDRESSES
# ------------------
@pytest.mark.parametrize("email", [
    # missing components
    "plainaddress",
    "missing-at-sign.com",
    "@nouser.com",
    "user@",
    # missing or too short TLD
    "user@example",
    "user@example.c",
    # invalid characters
    "user!@example.com",
    "user@exa mple.com",
    "user @example.com",
    # whitespace / control characters
    "user@example.com\n",
    " user@example.com ",
    # unicode
    "用户@例子.公司",
])
def test_invalid_emails(email):
    assert not is_valid_email(email)


# ------------------
# EDGE CASES THE REGEX WILL ACTUALLY ACCEPT
# (even though real-world email rules might reject them)
# ------------------
@pytest.mark.parametrize("email", [
    # local part starting or ending with a dot
    ".leadingdot@example.com",
    "trailingdot.@example.com",
    # consecutive dots in local or domain
    "double..dots@example.com",
    "user@example..com",
    # domain starting with a dot
    "user@.example.com",
])
def test_weird_but_allowed_by_regex(email):
    # according to our regex implementation these are all True
    assert is_valid_email(email)


# ------------------
# NON-STRING INPUTS SHOULD BUBBLE UP A TYPE ERROR
# ------------------
@pytest.mark.parametrize("bad_input", [
    None,
    123,
    ["user@example.com"],
    b"user@example.com",
])
def test_non_string_input_raises_type_error(bad_input):
    with pytest.raises(TypeError):
        is_valid_email(bad_input)
```

Explanation of what’s covered:

- `test_valid_emails` exercises a variety of “normal” addresses, including minimal lengths and mixed case.  
- `test_invalid_emails` tries clearly malformed addresses (missing `@`, missing user or domain parts, too-short TLD, illegal characters, whitespace, Unicode) and asserts `False`.  
- `test_weird_but_allowed_by_regex` documents known‐oddities of this particular pattern (leading/trailing dots, consecutive dots, domain labels starting with a dot), demonstrating they return `True` even though RFC-compliant validators would reject them.  
- `test_non_string_input_raises_type_error` ensures passing non‐string values bubbles up the `TypeError` from `re.match`.
